rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's forgetting of a verse is by God's will, not a fault of his.
rows.anchor: because God willed it, not because of a fault on the part of the Prophet

rows.speaker: Muslims
rows.claim: Muslims believe God abrogated some verses and caused others to be forgotten, replacing them with better verses.
rows.anchor: Muslims believe that God abrogated some verses and caused others to be “forgotten,”

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: One interpretation is that God eases the way by making revealed law uncomplicated.
rows.anchor: Some understand this verse as an allusion to the uncomplicated nature of the revealed law

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: In context of the preceding verses, God makes it easy for the Prophet to memorize the Quran.
rows.anchor: in light of vv. 6–7, this verse indicates that God will make it easy for the Prophet to memorize the Quran

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that God eases believers' way into Paradise.
rows.anchor: Others interpret the verse as a reference to God’s easing the way for believers to enter Paradise

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: People should be reminded of God's message whether or not the reminder benefits them, because all will be held accountable.
rows.anchor: whether it is of benefit or not, all should be reminded of God’s message (Bg)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those certain of returning to God, and those who admit it without certainty, fear God; deniers of the return are the most wretched.
rows.anchor: Those who are certain of the return to God and those who admit to it but are not certain of it are those who fear God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In relation to the preceding verse, the reminder benefits only those who fear God.
rows.anchor: these verses imply that the reminder only benefits those who fear God

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The greatest Fire is the Hereafter's Fire, contrasted with the lesser fire of this world.
rows.anchor: The “greatest” or “greater” Fire is that of the Hereafter, while the lesser fire is that of this world

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Alternatively, the verse distinguishes degrees of punishment, with the worst Fire destined for the most wretched.
rows.anchor: Alternately, v. 12 alludes to different degrees of punishment, with the greatest Fire being that for which the most wretched are destined

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic idiom of neither living nor dying describes the experience of great trials.
rows.anchor: In Arabic, to say that one neither lives nor dies is to indicate that one is suffering great trials

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: One interpretation is that purification means escaping idolatry by professing God's Oneness.
rows.anchor: According to some, He indeed prospers who is purified refers to purification from idolatry by professing God’s Oneness

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Another interpretation is purification through good deeds.
rows.anchor: Others say that it refers to purification through good deeds

rows.speaker: still others
rows.claim: A further interpretation identifies purification with the alms given for ʿĪd al-fiṭr.
rows.anchor: still others say it refers specifically to the alms given on ʿĪd al-fiṭr

rows.speaker: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq
rows.claim: The sixth Imam says the verse order refers to alms being given in the morning before the two cycles of the ʿĪd prayer.
rows.anchor: the sixth Imam, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq, stated that the order of the verses refers to the alms being given in the morning

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Prayer here is usually understood as the five canonical prayers.
rows.anchor: Here prayer is taken by most as a reference to the five canonical prayers

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some instead understand prayer as the congregational prayer on the morning of ʿĪd al-fiṭr.
rows.anchor: by some as a reference to the congregational prayer said on the morning of ʿĪd al-fiṭr

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Remembering God's Name can mean uttering the basmalah at the beginning of each prayer.
rows.anchor: According to some, remembers the Name of his Lord refers to mentioning the Name of God in the basmalah at the beginning of each prayer

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others stress that remembrance must engage both heart and tongue; tongue-only remembrance without attention of heart has no benefit or reward.
rows.anchor: others emphasize that it means to remember with both heart and tongue, as remembering God with the tongue while being heedless of God in the heart has no benefit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read together, the verses describe whole-person worship: purifying the heart, remembering God with the tongue, and performing God's commands, especially prayer.
rows.anchor: These two verses can be taken together as referring to worshipping with all aspects of one’s being

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some take the address about preferring worldly life to be directed at disbelievers.
rows.anchor: According to some, you is here an address to the disbelievers

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others take the address to include all humanity.
rows.anchor: while others say that it refers to all of humanity

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith compares the world to a prison for the believer and a garden for the disbeliever.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth states, “The world is the prison of the believer and the garden of the disbeliever”

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The reference to old scriptures may concern the subjects discussed in verses 14–17.
rows.anchor: This refers to either the subjects mentioned in vv. 14–17

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that it refers to the whole of this surah.
rows.anchor: the whole of this sūrah

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Another interpretation applies the reference to the entire Quran, as verse 26:196 does.
rows.anchor: or the entire Quran, as in 26:196

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Judaism and Christianity do not assign Abraham a revealed book, the Quran and hadith imply that he had a scripture.
rows.anchor: Although Judaism and Christianity do not ascribe a revealed book to Abraham, that Abraham had a particular scripture is implied in both the Quran and the Ḥadīth

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A report attributes to the Prophet a total of 104 revealed books: 50 to Seth, 30 to Idrīs, 10 to Abraham, 10 to Moses before the Torah, plus Torah, Gospel, Psalms, and Quran.
rows.anchor: When the Prophet was asked how many revealed books there were, he responded

rows.speaker: Shiite sources
rows.claim: Shiite sources give a slightly different narration, and some say Abraham received 20 scrolls.
rows.anchor: This tradition has a slightly different narration in Shiite sources

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah was revealed in Mecca and takes its name from the overwhelming event, usually understood as Resurrection.
rows.anchor: the overwhelming event in the first verse, which most maintain refers to the Day of Resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah develops the believers-disbelievers contrast of 87:11–15, describing Hell, then the Garden, creation's signs, and the Prophet's limited role as warner.
rows.anchor: It can be seen as related to the previous sūrah insofar as it elaborates upon the dichotomy between the believers and the disbelievers

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to have often recited this surah with the previous one at Friday congregational prayer.
rows.anchor: It is reported that the Prophet would often recite this sūrah during the Friday congregational prayer along with the previous sūrah

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: The opening may be rendered as a declarative statement that the audience has heard tell of the event.
rows.anchor: The beginning of the verse can also be rendered, “Thou hast heard tell”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If read as a question, it is rhetorical and serves emphasis.
rows.anchor: If understood as a question, it is rhetorical, for emphasis

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: The overwhelming event most likely means Resurrection, whose grandeur overwhelms humanity.
rows.anchor: the overwhelming event most likely refers to the Day of Resurrection, whose grandeur will overcome all of humanity

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Alternative readings identify the event with Hell covering people in layers or Fire overwhelming disbelievers' faces.
rows.anchor: it is also taken by some to mean that Hell will “cover” or “overwhelm” the people in layers

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The humbled faces are abased or humiliated.
rows.anchor: Here, humbled means abased or humiliated

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Unlike worldly humility, humiliation in the Hereafter benefits disbelievers nothing because repentance is possible only in this world.
rows.anchor: Unlike humility that one experiences in this world, this humility will reportedly be of no benefit to disbelievers

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Toil and weariness may refer to work in the Fire, such as dragging chains and shackles, or futile toil in worldly opposition to God.
rows.anchor: Toiling, weary can be understood as a reference to their toil in the scorching Fire

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Another view assigns toil to disobedience in this world and weariness to suffering in the Fire.
rows.anchor: Others see toiling as a reference to performing disobedient acts in this world and weary as a reference to suffering in the Fire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taṣlā, rendered entering, also has a reading tuṣlā, meaning made to enter.
rows.anchor: can also be read Tuṣlā, meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boiling spring is water at the highest possible heat, contrasting with the Garden's flowing spring.
rows.anchor: Boiling spring refers to water at the highest possible heat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍarīʿ is the dry form of shibrīq, a bitter thorny desert shrub, so vile no animal eats it.
rows.anchor: Vile thorn translates ḍarīʿ, which is the name given to the dry version of a bitter and thorny desert shrub

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some identify ḍarīʿ as a tree in the Fire, similar to Zaqqūm.
rows.anchor: Some say that it designates a tree of the Fire (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Hadith
rows.claim: A hadith describes ḍarīʿ in the Fire as thorn-like, bitterer than aloes, more fetid than a corpse, and hotter than fire.
rows.anchor: Ḍarīʿ is a thing in the Fire that resembles thorns. It is bitterer than aloes, more fetid than a putrid corpse

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some interpret ḍarīʿ as poison.
rows.anchor: Some say ḍarīʿ means “poison”

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others derive the word from ḍaraʿa, to humble or abase, because eating it humiliates those in the Fire.
rows.anchor: Others say that it derives from the verb ḍaraʿa, meaning “to humble” or “to abase,”

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most distinguish ḍarīʿ from Zaqqūm and filth, treating these as vegetation of different levels of Hell.
rows.anchor: Most commentators agree that it is not the same as other things the disbelievers will be made to eat in Hell

rows.speaker: Arabs
rows.claim: After Arabs said their camels were nourished by ḍarīʿ, actually the pre-dried shibrīq, this verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: It is related that in response to v. 6 the Arabs said, “Our camels are nourished by ḍarīʿ,” though it was actually shibrīq

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of blessed faces in the Hereafter is connected to other Quranic descriptions of faces.
rows.anchor: For characteristics of faces in the Hereafter, see

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike the fruitless deeds of the toil-worn in 88:3, these people will realize and enjoy the results of their labor.
rows.anchor: In contrast to those whose deeds bear no fruit in the Hereafter in v. 3, those referred to in this verse will realize and enjoy the fruits of their labor

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Paradise contains no vain discourse.
rows.anchor: In Paradise there be will no vain discourse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading takes the faces mentioned in verse 8 as the verb's subject.
rows.anchor: Here they is based upon reading the faces in v. 8 as the subject of the verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase may address the Prophet in second person: thou hearest no idle talk there.
rows.anchor: It could also be understood as an address to the Prophet in the second person singular

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant makes the verb passive, with idle talk as the subject.
rows.anchor: In another variant, the verb is read in the passive with idle talk as the subject

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: The singular spring may be read generically to indicate many springs in Heaven.
rows.anchor: Spring can be read as having a generic import indicating a multitude of springs in heaven

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The couches are the same as the embroidered couches in 56:15; those seated there have rancor removed from their breasts.
rows.anchor: These are the same as the embroidered couches mentioned in 56:15

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Goblets allude to the wine of Paradise that they contain.
rows.anchor: The mention of goblets in the Quran is taken as an allusion to the wine of Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Camels, mountains, sky, and earth dominate desert life; reflection on created signs should suffice to reveal the truth.
rows.anchor: These verses indicate that reflecting upon the signs of God in the created order should suffice to make one understand the truth

rows.speaker: Bg, IK, Ṭs
rows.claim: Camels are readily domesticated, provide food, milk, and transport, bear heavy loads, and survive with little water and thorny brush; they exemplify God's Wisdom and Power.
rows.anchor: Camels were central to desert livelihood, as they were easy to domesticate; could be eaten, milked, or used as beasts of burden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel may also exemplify docility: despite its strength it yields to its guide, unlike humans who resist God's guidance.
rows.anchor: The reference to camels can also be understood as an allusion to the docile nature of camels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The raised sky is linked to verse 50:6.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Firm mountains evidence God's Power and Mercy; their mention often accompanies the earth's spread and its benefits to people.
rows.anchor: The mountains being made firm is cited as evidence of God’s Power and Mercy in several verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's role is to remind; he is not responsible for others' faith or disbelief and cannot create faith in their hearts.
rows.anchor: The Prophet’s mission is only to remind people of the truth. He will not be held responsible for the faith or disbelief of others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God holds judgment and reckoning.
rows.anchor: That judgment and reckoning lie with God alone is also mentioned in

rows.speaker: Ṭb
rows.claim: Commentators have proposed as many as thirty-six interpretations of even and odd.
rows.anchor: Commentators have given this verse up to thirty-six different interpretations

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Even can denote all created pairs and odd God as the One without peer.
rows.anchor: Some interpret even as a reference to all of creation, for as 78:6–8 says, Did We not . . . create you in pairs

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A saying attributed to the Prophet interprets even and odd as the prayer cycles: most prayers have an even count, while sunset prayer has an odd count.
rows.anchor: According to a saying attributed to the Prophet, this verse refers to the prayers

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: One interpretation takes odd as the Day of ʿArafah and even as either the eighth or tenth day of pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: Others say that odd refers to the Day of ʿArafah, which is the ninth day of the ḥajj

rows.speaker: other interpreters
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies odd with Adam and even with Eve.
rows.anchor: According to other interpretations, the odd refers to Adam, and the even to Eve

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: One reading pairs even Ṣafā and Marwah, traversed during pilgrimage, with odd as the Kaʿbah.
rows.anchor: the even refers to Ṣafā and Marwah, between which the pilgrims pass during the pilgrimage, and the odd refers to the Kaʿbah

rows.speaker: Shiite interpretation
rows.claim: A Shiite reading identifies even with ʿAlī and Fāṭimah and odd with the Prophet.
rows.anchor: One Shiite interpretation maintains that the even refers to ʿAlī and Fāṭimah and the odd refers to the Prophet himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿĀd were a pre-Islamic southern Arabian tribe who rejected the Prophet Hūd; their account is related elsewhere.
rows.anchor: a pre-Islamic southern Arabian tribe who rejected the Prophet Hūd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iram may denote either the people or the city of ʿĀd.
rows.anchor: Iram is believed to refer to either a particular people or

rows.speaker: some sources
rows.claim: Arabian legend says Shaddād, son of ʿĀd, built the city with gold, silver, and trees bearing jewels.
rows.anchor: Several sources cite the Arabian legend that this city was built by Shaddād, the son of ʿĀd, with gold and silver

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: A genealogy identifies ʿĀd as son of ʿAwṣ, son of Iram, son of Sham, son of Noah; the tribal ancestor's name also named the tribe.
rows.anchor: Some say ʿĀd was a son of ʿAwṣ, the son of Iram, the son of Sham, the son of Noah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that account, Iram means ʿĀd the Former, while the later group was simply called ʿĀd; pillared describes their tall stature.
rows.anchor: Iram is then taken as a reference to ʿĀd the Former (53:50), while ʿĀd the Latter were simply referred to as ʿĀd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Iram denotes the city, pillared describes its architecture; it can also describe noble stature, as in the Arabic idiom rafīʿ al-ʿimād.
rows.anchor: If taken as a reference to a city where they lived, pillared refers to the architecture of their city

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamūd were a pre-Islamic northern Arabian tribe who rejected the Prophet Ṣāliḥ; their account is related elsewhere.
rows.anchor: a pre-Islamic northern Arabian tribe who rejected the Prophet Ṣāliḥ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possible meanings of Pharaoh's tent poles are discussed at 38:12.
rows.anchor: For the possible meanings of tent poles

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tyranny and corruption described apply to all three peoples named in verses 6–10.
rows.anchor: These verses refer to all three groups mentioned in vv. 6–10

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poured conveys that punishment continues in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: Poured indicates the continuous nature of the punishment that is realized in this life and the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawṭ means something mixed in different ways, hence a whip woven of diverse materials; it can describe punishment mixing blood and flesh or several kinds of punishment.
rows.anchor: Scourge translates sawṭ, which indicates something that is mixed in various ways

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three peoples suffered distinct punishments: a raging wind for ʿĀd, an overwhelming earthquake for Thamūd, and drowning for Pharaoh and his host.
rows.anchor: a howling, raging wind for the tribe of ʿĀd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nothing escapes God: He hears and sees public and private words and deeds and rewards or punishes accordingly; tyrants may be given respite but are punished in due time.
rows.anchor: no matter what respite God may allow for tyrants to work corruption, they will be punished for it in due time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People wrongly treat wealth and status as proof of worth before God, forgetting that God expands or constricts provision and that nobility is reverence.
rows.anchor: Human beings are inclined to think that wealth and status are marks of true worth or signs of one’s standing with God

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī links these verses to heedlessness about the Hereafter and to worship on a brink, showing that worldly good may harm in the next life and apparent abasement may become honor; attachment to sensory life makes departure harder.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī connects the present verses to 30:7

rows.speaker: God in a ḥadīth qudsī
rows.claim: God says worldly abundance or paucity does not itself honor or abase; honor comes through obedience and abasement through disobedience.
rows.anchor: I only honor one whom I have honored with obedience unto Me

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nay rebukes those who wrongly inferred divine favor or abasement from wealth; neglecting orphans and consuming their inheritance is one example of resulting injustice.
rows.anchor: Nay is a rebuke to those who make the errors implied in vv. 15–16

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: These verses may be read in third-person plural instead of second-person plural; either reading is accepted.
rows.anchor: Some read all of these verses in the third-person plural rather than the second-person plural

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Failure to understand God's true honoring and abasing leads people to treat the less privileged inequitably.
rows.anchor: the implication of vv.17–20 is that failure to appreciate the true nature of God’s honoring and abasing leads people to act inequitably toward those who are less privileged

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: The feeding exhortation has four readings: second-person transitive or reflexive, and third-person transitive or reflexive.
rows.anchor: It can be read in two ways in the second-person plural: transitive, taḥuḍḍūna

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With a third-person reading, the criticism applies to the people described in verses 15–16.
rows.anchor: When read in the third person, it is seen as applying to those mentioned in vv. 15–16

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Devouring inheritance means taking whatever one can find without checking whether it is lawful or forbidden, and consuming both one's own and others' shares.
rows.anchor: This verse means that people consume whatever they can find without knowing or questioning whether it is permitted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage condemns intense love of wealth, as elsewhere in the Quran.

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: The earth's repeated grinding means everything is destroyed and reduced to sand, as in a great earthquake.
rows.anchor: Ground up implies that all things have been destroyed and reduced to sand

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some understand the grinding as preparing a plain where all humans and jinn gather for Judgment.
rows.anchor: According to some this grinding will prepare the plain on which all human beings and jinn will then be gathered

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Since God has no body, location, or motion, some interpret God's coming as an allusion to divine Power, Decree, or Command.
rows.anchor: As God is not considered to have a body or be a “thing” that can be said to be in a particular place

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others understand the verse as God's Presence, with knowledge of Him becoming manifest on that Day even to deniers.
rows.anchor: Others say that it indicates God’s Presence

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The angels may stand in rows like Muslims at prayer.
rows.anchor: It is said that the angels will be lined up like Muslims in prayer

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Another view is that angels descend from every heaven and form lines around believers.
rows.anchor: Others say the angels will descend from every heaven forming lines around the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone punishes on Judgment Day, and no punishment compares with that Day's punishment; the chains and shackles are mentioned elsewhere.
rows.anchor: Ultimately, God will be the only one who punishes anyone on the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: Āl, Qu, R
rows.claim: An alternate reading says God punishes none with His punishment and binds none with His binding, so no one receives another's punishment or is punished as severely as disbelievers.
rows.anchor: Others read, “He punishes none with his punishment, and He binds none with his binding”

rows.speaker: Āl, R, Z
rows.claim: The claim that none bears another's burden may be general, applying to everyone.
rows.anchor: This interpretation could be general, meaning that no one suffers the punishment or binding due another, since none shall bear the burden of another

rows.speaker: Āl, Q, Z
rows.claim: Some apply the alternate interpretation to a particular individual, or to Satan.
rows.anchor: It could also be specific, applying to a particular individual

rows.speaker: Āl, Q, R, Sy
rows.claim: The address to the soul at peace is attributed either to angels or directly to God, and occurs at death or Resurrection.
rows.anchor: It is said that these verses are an address from the angels to human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses are prominent in Muslim funeral eulogies; Sufis see them as describing the soul's true nature once purified.
rows.anchor: They play an important role in Muslim piety, as they are often recited in eulogies for the dead

rows.speaker: Q, Qu, R
rows.claim: The soul at peace has certainty, like Abraham's heart at peace; it also possesses gnosis and rests in God's remembrance, with degrees of remembrance, certainty, and peace corresponding.
rows.anchor: The soul at peace is said to be the soul that has certainty

rows.speaker: Jurjānī
rows.claim: The soul is illuminated by the heart, its blameworthy traits removed and praiseworthy traits made manifest.
rows.anchor: Others speak of the soul so illuminated by the heart that all blameworthy character traits have been removed

rows.speaker: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb
rows.claim: Ubayy read the verse as addressing a secure soul at peace, implying immunity from fear and sorrow unlike those in verses 15–16.
rows.anchor: read this verse as “O thou soul secure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soul has three levels: the peaceful soul controls desires and has certainty, the blaming soul struggles against desire, and the soul commanding evil is ruled by desire.
rows.anchor: The soul is said to have three levels: the soul at peace (v. 27), which is in command of its lusts and desires

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: A Sufi description presents the peaceful soul as created by primordial divine light, at peace with God and His Address, and oriented solely toward witnessing God.
rows.anchor: Then its Lord calls it to its first origin

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The soul's return to its Lord may imply that it was with its Lord in the Garden before creation.
rows.anchor: That the soul returns to its Lord is understood to imply that it was with its Lord in the Garden before creation

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Many interpret content and contenting as satisfied with God's reward and pleasing to God for having done good deeds.
rows.anchor: Many interpret this verse to mean content with the reward of God and contenting to God for having performed good deeds

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others understand the phrase to mean accepting everything God has decreed.
rows.anchor: Others understand it as an indication that one is content with everything that God has decreed

rows.speaker: Aj, K
rows.claim: Some see return to the Divine Essence in complete contentment; content and contenting may express two levels, through God and before God.
rows.anchor: Still others take it as an indication that the soul returns to the Divine Essence in a state of complete contentment

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: Some stress that God must be content with souls before they can be content with Him.
rows.anchor: Some emphasize that there can be no contentment with God until God is content with souls

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: Contentment is described as a foremost virtue, the greatest gate of God and the paradise of this world.
rows.anchor: Contentment is seen by some as one of the most important virtues; it has been described as “the greatest gate of God and the paradise of this world”

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Entering among God's servants means joining the righteous, as in Solomon's supplication.
rows.anchor: Among My servants means among the righteous servants, as in the supplication of Solomon in 27:19

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: The phrase is read as an address to the spiritual elect.
rows.anchor: In this sense it is read as an address to the spiritual elect

rows.speaker: Q, R, Sy, Ṭs
rows.claim: Others read the phrase as entering into the servants' bodies, referring to spirits returning to bodies in bodily resurrection; some allow both readings.
rows.anchor: Some read, “Enter into My servants,” meaning their bodies, thus alluding to spirits returning to bodies for the bodily resurrection

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The Hereafter contains progressive levels, from lower to higher gardens; most take God's Garden as Paradise generally, while some identify it with the highest Garden of the Divine Essence in God's Presence.
rows.anchor: the Hereafter has progressive levels with lower and higher gardens

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some read the verse without Nay, taking lā as an emphatic particle rather than negation.
rows.anchor: Some read this verse without Nay, interpreting that the article lā as one of emphasis rather than negation

rows.speaker: Q, IK
rows.claim: If lā is negative, it rebukes the disposition criticized in verses 5–11 or rebukes Quraysh.
rows.anchor: When read as an article of negation, it can be seen as a rebuke to those who are of the disposition criticized in vv. 5–11

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Balad may mean Arabia, but most interpret it as the city of Mecca; minority readings identify Medina or the earth generally.
rows.anchor: Land, translating balad, can refer to Arabia, though a majority read it as “city,” referring to Makkah

rows.speaker: IK, Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Most take the verse to mean the Prophet is free to act as he wishes in Mecca, in response to its conquest or as a premonition of it.
rows.anchor: Most interpret this verse to mean that the Prophet is free to act as he deems best in Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading points to the conquest in 8/630, or forecasts it if the surah was revealed in Mecca, when Quraysh members were slain; bloodshed violated Mecca's pre-Islamic sanctuary.
rows.anchor: In this sense, it is seen as a direct response to the conquest of Makkah in 8/630 or, if revealed during the Makkan period, as a premonition of the conquest

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet said God made Mecca sacred at creation and permitted him alone to fight there for one hour, with no one before or after him given that permission.
rows.anchor: Truly God made Makkah sacred on the day that He created the heavens and the earth

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Others say God gave the Prophet free passage through Mecca despite Quraysh denying access to the Kaʿbah.
rows.anchor: Others say that this verse refers to God giving the Prophet free passage through Makkah, even if the Quraysh did not

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The verse may mean the Prophet is present in the land, honoring it by his presence.
rows.anchor: The verse could also be read, “And thou art present in the land,” alluding to the fact that this land has been honored by God with the presence of His Messenger

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The begetter and begotten may mean Adam and his descendants, or every parent and child, humanity from beginning to end.
rows.anchor: The begetter, and that which he begat means Adam and his progeny, or every begetter and every begotten

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the begetter and begotten as Abraham and Ishmael, connecting them to Mecca.
rows.anchor: Or the phrase can be seen as a reference to Abraham and Ishmael

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another reading takes Ishmael as the begetter and his progeny as the begotten, tying them to the land through Ishmael's paternity of Arabs.
rows.anchor: or to Ishmael and his progeny

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A metaphorical interpretation makes the begetter the Prophet and his community the begotten.
rows.anchor: Another metaphorical interpretation states that the begetter is the Prophet and that which he begat is his community

rows.speaker: ST
rows.claim: Some read the oath as alluding to the Prophet's descent from Abraham.
rows.anchor: Some also read it as an allusion to the Prophet’s descent from Abraham

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question concerns whether man expects accountability for all his acts; wealth-deluded people forget God controls provision and can remove it at any time, and answer for how they obtain and spend it regardless of philanthropy.
rows.anchor: V. 5 asks, “Does man not think that he will be held accountable for all his actions?”

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: Some identify the speaker as Ḥarith ibn ʿĀmir, who complained he had spent his wealth on expiations and payments since entering Muhammad's religion.
rows.anchor: Some have said that v. 6 refers to Ḥarith ibn ʿĀmir

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The question asks whether people think God will ask how they acquired and spent their wealth.
rows.anchor: This verse asks, “Do people think that God will not ask how they obtained their wealth and how they spent it?”

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: Some apply the verse to a person who falsely claimed to have spent money for Islam.
rows.anchor: Some say this refers to a specific individual who claimed to have spent money for Islam, though he had not spent anything

rows.speaker: Hadith
rows.claim: A hadith says a servant will be questioned at Resurrection about lifespan, the source and use of wealth, and knowledge put into practice.
rows.anchor: The servant does not move forward on the Day of Resurrection until he has been asked about three things

rows.speaker: Shiite version
rows.claim: A Shiite version adds a fourth question about love for the Prophet's Household.
rows.anchor: a Shiite version adds a fourth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The One capable of making subtle, beneficial instruments such as eyes, tongue, and lips can know every deed and hold people accountable for their use.
rows.anchor: one who is able to make these subtle instruments from which human beings derive great benefit would certainly be able to know every deed

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The two highways mean good and evil; a hadith urges people not to prefer the evil path, and commentators link the verse to God's guidance in 76:3.
rows.anchor: The two highways are interpreted to be those of good and evil

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith warns that there are only two paths, good and evil, and people should not make evil more beloved.
rows.anchor: O people! There are only two highways: the highway of good and the highway of evil

rows.speaker: R, Z
rows.claim: Iqtaḥama, translated assail, means acting with great intensity.
rows.anchor: Assail translates iqtaḥama, meaning to do something with great intensity

rows.speaker: Āl, Q
rows.claim: Iqtaḥama can alternatively mean throwing oneself into something without considering the consequences.
rows.anchor: or to throw oneself into something without consideration of the consequences

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who donate for religion and then regret it, or neglect comparable duties, lack full sincerity and gratitude for God's blessings; the steep pass is giving wealth and doing good deeds.
rows.anchor: those who contribute money for religious purposes, but then regret it, saying, I have squandered vast wealth

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: The steep pass is a metaphor for striving for God, including distributing wealth as in verses 13–17 and performing meritorious deeds.
rows.anchor: the steep pass is a metaphorical reference to distributing wealth in the manner mentioned in vv. 13–17

rows.speaker: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī
rows.claim: A saying attributed to al-Ḥasan calls the pass humanity's struggle against the soul, caprice, and Satan.
rows.anchor: The steep pass of God is severe; it is the human being’s striving against his soul, his caprice, and his enemy, Satan

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Others take the steep pass as one or more obstacles disbelievers face in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Some view the steep pass as an allusion to one or several of the obstacles that disbelievers will encounter in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Many read the question as asking what will apprise the Prophet of assailing the steep pass.
rows.anchor: many read v. 12 to mean, “What will apprise thee of assailing the steep pass?”

rows.speaker: al-Tustarī
rows.claim: Assailing the pass means attaining spiritual knowledge by God's power, which frees the soul of desire.
rows.anchor: Al-Tustarī likens assailing the steep pass to attaining spiritual knowledge

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: The verse urges two meritorious acts: generosity toward both an orphan and relatives.
rows.anchor: This verse constitutes two meritorious acts, as one should be generous toward orphans and toward relatives

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most say an orphan is one whose father has died; some include loss of both parents.
rows.anchor: Most maintain that orphan

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: An indigent clinging to dust is someone with no home other than the dust.
rows.anchor: An indigent is one who has no home other than the dust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The companions of the right are in Paradise, while those of the left are in the Fire.
rows.anchor: For the companions of the right, who are said to be in Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The symbolism of right and left is also developed elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: For the symbolic distinction between right and left, also see

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs
rows.claim: Enclosed means locked: Hell's doors shut on disbelievers, barring escape; distress is not lifted and no spirit enters.
rows.anchor: Enclosed here means locked, for the doors of Hell have been locked upon the disbelievers so that they cannot leave

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muʾsadah, translated enclosed, can also mean covered over.
rows.anchor: Enclosed translates muʾsadah, which can also mean

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some reject the rendering the One Who, saying God cannot swear by Himself; they instead read that which.
rows.anchor: According to some, the One Who in these three verses is not appropriate, since God could not swear upon Himself

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī prefers reading the verses as nominal phrases: its establishing, its spreading, and its fashioning.
rows.anchor: the reading preferred by al-Qurṭubī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse can mean God taught the soul good and evil and set its course; alternatively, He instilled iniquity and reverence in it.
rows.anchor: As translated, this verse indicates that God taught the soul the nature of evil and good

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both readings indicate God's instilling moral knowledge in every soul even before prophetic revelation; souls know right, wrong, their relation to God, and the primordial covenant.
rows.anchor: it can be taken as a reference to God’s instillation of the knowledge of good and evil in every human soul

rows.speaker: most Ashʿarite theologians
rows.claim: Another interpretation, preferred by most Ashʿarite theologians, is that God decrees all things for each human being.
rows.anchor: These verses can also be read as an indication that God decrees all things for each human being

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: In a report, the Prophet says human actions and struggles are ordained; God makes easy the path to Paradise or Hell for those created for either destination.
rows.anchor: So the man said, “Then what is the point of our actions?” The Prophet replied

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: When reciting the surah, the Prophet reportedly paused here to pray that God grant the soul reverence and purify it.
rows.anchor: when reciting this sūrah, the Prophet would stop at this verse and pray

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses inspired extensive writing on purification of the soul, regarded by some as the Quran's entire purpose.
rows.anchor: These two verses have served as the inspiration for extensive literature on the “purification of the soul”

rows.speaker: Bg, Sh
rows.claim: Most take verse 9 to begin the answer to the oaths in verses 1–7; others say the answer is omitted and implied.
rows.anchor: Most take v. 9 to be the beginning of the answer to the oaths taken in vv. 1–7

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The verses describe cleansing lowly traits and, conversely, dulling the soul through heedlessness and disobedience.
rows.anchor: The text speaks of those who cleanse the soul of lowly and despicable character traits

rows.speaker: IK, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some early commentators make God the subject: the soul God purifies prospers, and the soul He obscures fails.
rows.anchor: According to some of the earliest commentators, these two verses could also be read with God as the subject

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The subject's ambiguity can express cooperation between God and people: people purify themselves for their own souls while willing only as God wills; God purifies whom He will, yet changes a people when they change themselves.
rows.anchor: The ambiguity of the subject can also be seen as an allusion to the cooperation between God and human beings

rows.speaker: Sh, Z
rows.claim: The literal meanings are to grow for purify and to bury for obscure; the verses can be rendered whoever grows the soul prospers, whoever buries it fails.
rows.anchor: The literal meaning of purify
